acceptedAnswer.text: Customer lifetime value is the total profit a business can expect from a single customer over the whole time they keep buying. It is not one order, it is every order that customer will ever place, minus the cost of serving them. Because it looks past the first sale, CLV is what tells you how much you can afford to spend to acquire a customer in the first place.

CLV = average order value x purchase frequency per year x customer lifespan in years x gross margin. With a 100 EUR average order, 4 orders a year, a 3 year lifespan and a 20% margin, CLV is 240 EUR. This calculator uses the same formula but derives the lifespan from your retention rate, since 1 / (1 - retention) is easier to source from your own data than a lifespan in years.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between CLV and LTV?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is none. CLV stands for customer lifetime value and LTV for lifetime value, and the two acronyms are used interchangeably across e-commerce and SaaS. The distinction that actually matters is revenue CLV versus margin CLV: the same customer can look worth 600 EUR on revenue and 270 EUR on margin. Always compare a margin CLV with your acquisition cost.

mainEntity.name: What is a good CLV for an e-commerce store?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends entirely on your category. General dropshipping stores usually land between 50 and 150 EUR, fashion between 150 and 300 EUR, beauty between 200 and 400 EUR, electronics between 300 and 600 EUR, and supplements between 400 and 800 EUR because they are consumed and reordered. A CLV is only good or bad relative to your acquisition cost, never on its own.

mainEntity.name: What is a good CLV:CAC ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three to one is the accepted minimum. A customer should bring in three times what they cost to acquire, with the remainder covering fixed costs, logistics and risk. Between 1.5:1 and 3:1 you are viable but tight. Below 1.5:1 the model does not hold, and below 1:1 every new sale makes the loss bigger. Above 5:1 you are probably under-spending on acquisition.

mainEntity.name: How do I find my average order value (AOV)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide total revenue by the number of orders over the same period. 50,000 EUR of revenue across 500 orders is a 100 EUR average order value. In Shopify you will find it under Analytics, then Reports, in the sales reports. Use a full quarter rather than a single week so that one promotion does not distort the number.

mainEntity.name: How do I find my purchase frequency?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide the number of orders over a year by the number of unique customers who ordered in that year. Two hundred orders from a hundred customers is a frequency of 2. Shopify reports it under Analytics, Reports, in the customer behaviour section, alongside your repeat purchase rate. If you have less than a year of history, extrapolate carefully rather than optimistically.

mainEntity.name: How do I find my customer lifespan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Customer lifespan is 1 divided by your annual churn rate, which is the same as 1 / (1 - retention rate). If 30% of your customers never come back in a year, your lifespan is 1 / 0.30, that is 3.3 years. This calculator asks for retention instead of lifespan and does the conversion for you, because retention is a number you can pull from your own order history.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate CLV in Excel or Google Sheets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Build five columns: customer ID, average order value, purchase frequency, lifespan in years and gross margin. In the sixth column multiply the four values, for example =B2*C2*D2*E2. Drag it down your customer list and you get a CLV per customer, which lets you sort by value and see how concentrated your profit really is.

mainEntity.name: How does profit margin affect CLV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Directly and proportionally. Margin is a multiplier in the formula, so moving from 20% to 30% margin lifts CLV by half. It is also the reason a revenue-based CLV is misleading: a customer worth 600 EUR in revenue at a 45% margin is worth 270 EUR to you, and the difference is what decides whether a 120 EUR acquisition cost is sane.

mainEntity.name: How can I increase my customer lifetime value?

acceptedAnswer.text: Four levers, in order of speed. Raise the average order value with bundles, upsells and a free shipping threshold. Raise purchase frequency with post-purchase email flows, loyalty and subscriptions. Cut churn with a better post-purchase experience and win-back campaigns. And pick products that are reordered by nature, because a catalogue of one-shot items caps your CLV before you start.

Predictive CLV uses probabilistic models, typically BG/NBD paired with a Gamma-Gamma model for order value, to estimate how many more times each customer will buy and how much they will spend. It is more accurate than a flat average and it is what large retailers run. It also needs clean transaction history and a data pipeline, so for most stores the simple formula is the right starting point.

Yes, and it matters more there than anywhere else. Dropshipping margins are thin and acquisition costs keep rising, so a model that only breaks even on the first order dies quickly. Knowing your CLV tells you whether you can afford your current cost per acquisition, and pushes you towards products that get reordered instead of products that sell once.

mainEntity.name: How often should I recalculate my CLV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Once a quarter is enough for most stores, plus any time you change pricing, product mix, shipping policy or retention strategy. If you are scaling ad spend aggressively, recalculate monthly: your acquisition cost moves faster than your retention, and the ratio between the two is what tells you when to stop.
